subsubtopic: APPOINTMENT OF REVIEW COMMITTEE-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, Mr. Justice Dubin has recommended the establishment of an independent aviation safety board reporting to Parliament through other than the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin). A review Committee is to consider this recommendation. Virtually every member of the aviation community welcomes and endorses the Dubin recommendation with the singular exception, I suppose, of the air administrators. The evidence presented to the commission virtually commands such independence. With such widespread support the naming of the air administrator to the implementation team can only undermine the trust and confidence that can, if properly handled, result in the new safety board. Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Prince Edward-Hastings (Mr. Ellis):
That this House indicates its serious doubts about the conflict of interest which the appointment of the air administrator brings to the deliberations of the committee, and calls on the Minister of Transport to review his decision and replace this nominee with an acceptable representative of the operational level categories in the industry; and further calls on the minister to make a statement on motions setting forth those parts of the report with which he disagrees and has decided require further and delaying study.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity pursuant to the provisions of Standing Order 43, to move a motion which I believe will receive consent as the official
spokesmen of all parties have been made aware of this motion and appear to agree with it.
In view of the fact that the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry must report today on the main estimates, thereby ending its reference from this House, and whereas many serious problems pertaining to the west coast fishery necessitate further intensive consideration by the committee before this House rises, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Gaspe (Mr. Cyr):
That the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry be granted a special reference by this House to meet and to travel to the west coast during the month of June so that committee members may be able to meet with the minister's advisory board and fishermen's groups, to observe hearings of the Pearse Commission of Inquiry, to visit a number of salmonid enhancement projects and environmentally sensitive areas, and generally to become more acquainted with the operations of the Pacific coast fishery, all of which will help the committee to appreciate better the serious problems being experienced by west coast fishermen.

Madam Speaker, I rise on a matter of some urgency under the provisions of Standing Order 43. The Housing and Urban Development Association of Canada indicated yesterday that hundreds of builders are being forced into bankruptcy by a serious slump in the construction industry, arising from record high mortgage rates. Many builders have gone out of business in the past two years and, lately, hundreds have just disappeared.
In light of the fact that HUDAC has forecast that by the end of this year housing starts in Canada will be 8 per cent below their January forecast of 179,500 units to 165,000 units, and that it estimates 220,000 housing starts per year are needed to satisfy demand, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Lewis):

FUNDS FOR RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT-MOTION UNDER
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43. On last February 3 the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan), for political reasons, turned down Bill C-245 which would have set up a trust fund for research and development into cereal grain and oilseeds suitable for cultivation in western Canada, utilizing some $9 million of producers' money held by the government in a non-interest bearing account known as the Prairie Farm Emergency Fund. subsubtopic: DUB1N INQUIRY REPORT-REASONS FOR APPOINTMENT OF REVIEW COMMITTEE
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Transport. When Mr. Justice Dubin was appointed to conduct an inquiry into air safety by the former minister of transport, the hon. member for Vegreville, it was seen by all as the most forward step in aviation history since the Aeronautics Act was written. Now that the report has been tabled and the weight of public opinion, both in the industry and the general public, has given it unanimous support, what is there about the report that makes the Minister of Transport want to hide behind a committee which is to review the report, especially a committee with a majority of obviously biased members, instead of accepting the report and its recommendations?

subsubtopic: DUB1N INQUIRY REPORT-REASONS FOR APPOINTMENT OF REVIEW COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I do not agree at all with the hon. member's commentary. The general reaction has been very favourable to the members whom I have appointed to the advisory committee. Mr. Baldwin has tremendous experience as a transportation administrator. Mr. Deschenes is a top-notch lawyer with expertise both in marine and air matters. Mr. Reid is a former pilot who is also very knowledgeable. Mr. Michaud has much experience in running an airline and Mr. Wilkins is generally accepted as the chairman of that group. The only unfavourable reaction I have had from the press is with regard to the appointment of Mr. McLeish, the air administrator.
In this regard, I appeal to my hon. friend's sense of balance and wisdom. The effect of not having the air administrator represented on that committee would have resulted in receiving advice from two sides, namely, from the department and the advisory committee. As I wanted to act quickly in this matter, presumably I would have had to look for a third source of advice or make decisions on my own knowledge, and I am sure the hon. member would not agree with me doing that. I will, however, make those decisions but I want to have reconciled and knowledgeable advice from all sides, not from one single entity and that is why Mr. McLeish is on the advisory committee.

Madam Speaker, the Minister of Transport really did not answer my question. I asked him why he does not accept the report and its recommendations right now.
I think the report of Mr. Justice Dubin was one of the best reports we have seen. Certainly there is a tremendous amount of public objection to Mr. McLeish being on the committee, but if the minister is not going to accept the report as it is written right now, why does he insist on having Mr. McLeish on the committee instead of naming someone to this committee from such air organizations as CALPA, COPA, ATAC and all of the rest?

Madam Speaker, I tried to avoid appointing representatives of different agencies, unions or companies to that committee, and that is why I chose people who were retired or had severed their relationships with the entities with which they had been associated.
On the hon. member's main question as to why 1 do not accept the whole of that report and call it quits, 1 do not think that makes sense. That would be giving to a report-however good it is, and everyone agrees that it makes a major contribution-a sort of biblical value. 1 do not think Mr. Justice Dubin would agree with that. As a matter of fact I suspect that today he would like to rewrite some of the pages.
It is normal and standard practice, when a government calls for a report of this kind, to analyse it, to get the best expertise and to be discriminate in the way it treats the report. I am aware of some reports treated that way. What we are doing now is getting the best advice possible.
Previous bills on the same subject, in particular Bill C-40, were introduced. We will now compare previous bills with the recommendations made by Mr. Justice Dubin and try to select the best.

Are there any fiscal transfer payments other than the established programs financing formula and the fiscal equalization programs and, if so, what are they and what is the per capita amount by province?

In addition to established programs financing and fiscal equalization, fiscal transfer payments to provincial governments in 1981-82 include statutory subsidies, the public utilities income tax transfer, reciprocal taxation payments, transfers under the 1971 undistributed income on hand program, and the Youth Allowance recovery.
Statutory subsidies are the oldest fiscal transfers and are paid as part of the terms of Confederation. They take several forms, including a grant in support of provincial legislatures, a per capita grant, a debt allowance and certain special grants.
Under the Public Utilities Income Tax Transfer Act (PUITTA) the federal government pays to provinces 95 per cent of the tax collected from corporations involved in the distribution or generation for distribution of electrical energy, gas and steam to the public.
Through the reciprocal taxation agreements provinces which have agreed to do so pay federal consumption taxes on their purchases of goods and services, and the federal government makes payments in lieu of provincial consumption taxes and fees on its purchases of goods and services in these provinces. Six provinces-Newfoundland, Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Quebec and Ontario-are currently participating in these arrangements.
Under the Income Tax Act corporations could distribute, tax free, to shareholders profits accumulated prior to 1972, once the special federal tax was paid. This payment represents the provincial share of the tax collected, and the 1981-82 transfer effectively winds up the program.
The Youth Allowances program has expired; however, the federal government continues to transfer three personal income tax points to Quebec and their value is recovered by means of a reduction in amounts otherwise payable to the province.

Madam Speaker, I am grateful for two reasons to be able to address myself to this legislation. Although it has been a subject of bills before in the House, one might say that I have been waiting around for over 23 years to speak on legislation that has not been much altered since 1908 when it was first passed. The second reason is that it gives me one of those typical opportunities to address myself to a measure in a totally non-partisan way.
The government introduced this legislation last February. It repeals the Juvenile Delinquents Act which is some 73 years old. There has been very little change since it was first passed in 1908.
I want to do three things with the time available to me. I want to compare the legislation before us with the archaic and outmoded Juvenile Delinquents Act. Also I want to compare the legislation before us with that which was introduced during the short time the Progressive Conservative Party held office; that is, the legislation introduced by the hon. member for Durham-Northumberland (Mr. Lawrence), the then solicitor general, in October 1979.
Generally the legislation is not only welcomed by our party, but we support it very strongly in principle. There are some areas in the legislation now before us which require somewhat closer scrutiny than they have had. Perhaps the most obvious deficiency of the bill is its very title. A shortcoming of the Juvenile Delinquents Act, which is the existing legislation governing the manner in which we deal with young people in the judicial process, is that it stigmatized young people at the outset. The new legislation does not meet this hurdle. Its short title, the Young Offenders Act, does not help us. It merely perpetuates a problem which could quite easily be overcome. This was pointed out by the hon. member for Halifax West
May 29, 1981

(Mr. Crosby) when he spoke during second reading stage in April of this year.
One of the purposes of this bill is to give a fresh start to or to take a fresh direction in the manner in which we deal with young people in conflict with the law. For instance, in connection with my remarks as to the title, we have no adult offenders act. There is no implication that an adult charged under the provisions of the Criminal Code is predestined to be found guilty. It is called the Criminal Code; under the fundamental principles of our system of justice, everyone is deemed to be innocent until proven guilty. This disappears by implication in the title of this bill. I do not think we should have a bill which prestigmatizes young people by implication in the title of the legislation itself. Perhaps a better title for the legislation, which might be considered in committee, is the "youth justice act" or some similar title which contains no implication or stigmatization of young people.
One of the major criticisms of the bill concerns the age limitation. The minimum age of criminal responsibility under the Criminal Code is seven years. Under clause 2(1) of the bill, the minimum age is raised to 12 years. In the 1975 report which was entitled "Young Persons in Conflict with the Law", the minimum age suggested was 14, but subsequently it was lowered to 12 by the proposals of the solicitor general in 1977. The age of 12 was also favoured by our government during its short term in office.
Although there are unavoidable difficulties in establishing a minimum age, a higher minimum age could well be argued so as to emphasize the contribution which welfare and educational techniques could make in dealing with children, as well as the importance of avoiding the stigma attached to a judicial hearing. The effect of raising the minimum age is that young people between the ages of seven and 12 will now be subject to provincial and territorial laws. This raises the question of provincial and territorial responsibilities to these young people.
Thus far the government has not said whether there will be any increased funding for the expansion of child welfare services which will inevitably occur. It is not clear how the provinces and the territories will respond to the jurisdictional void which will occur, but it is relatively certain that there will be a wide variation in approaches, which according to my prediction will also lead to inequities in the dispensation of the effects of this legislation.
Hopefully, when the minister closes the debate he will address the subject of the financial aspect of implementing the proposed new minimum age limit. Consideration must also be given to the manner in which provincial and territorial offenders will be processed. The bill before us is absolutely silent as to this aspect of the matter.
A serious inequity arises in relation to the maximum age set; or perhaps it is more appropriate to say "not set" by Bill C-61. The provision is for a maximum age of 18 years. However, this may be lowered by the provinces and the territories to 16 or 17. This could lead to something which the government, in other pieces of legislation, has been attempting to avoid like the plague-a checkerboard effect throughout the country
Young Offenders Act
which does nothing for the uniform dispensation of law in the country, particularly criminal law.
Section 15 of the proposed charter of rights protects against discrimination on the basis of age. The legislation should be attempting to bring uniformity to this area of law. Young people throughout Canada, no matter where they reside, should have available to them the provisions of this bill, although the age of majority varies from jurisdiction to jurisdiction. The possibility of discrimination in relation to the application of the law raises the issue with which the charter of rights is supposed to deal. It does not appear that the government, which is presumably committed to its new constitutional proposal, has clearly thought out the effect of these provisions; in my submission they are in direct conflict.
The government appears to have failed to relate its constitutional proposal, particularly the inclusion of a charter of rights, to the business which it is now presenting to the House for approval. Under the present proposal, a 17-year-old youth in one province or territory could fall within the sphere or the ambit of the provisions of this legislation, whereas in another province or territory the same youth may fall within the provisions of the Criminal Code and be treated as an adult with all the possible harsh consequences which could ensue from that circumstance.
Surely this is not acceptable; surely it should be remedied before the bill becomes law. The Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs should very closely and carefully examine this inconsistency. It is not simply an apparent inconsistency; it is one in fact.
Also the bill before us provides for alternate measures to the court process laid out in clause 4. It is a welcome provision, as not all youths who break federal laws will have to appear in youth courts. It has long been recognized that the courts are often full of youths, young people who should not be there, just as our penitentiary system is full of young people, many of whom should not be there.
These provisions give formal recognition to the voluntary- and I emphasize that word-performance of community service or restitution to the victim in lieu of a court appearance. Nothing in the provisions of the bill preclude or bar proceedings against the youth in a court where innocence or guilt may be established. The main criticism which I have of this section is that there is no formal process established in the administration of these diversion techniques, even though I recognize that diversion throughout the country, and particularly more so in some parts of the country than others, is in the experimental process.
Surely in this legislation the techniques, the process itself, should be spelled out. Although safeguards exist to ensure that the youth is dealt with equitably, if diversion is used the process by which this occurs is not governed by even the vaguest of guidelines. It falls totally within the powers of the provinces and territories. Perhaps that is the intention. But, once again, we could find ourselves faced with inequities

May 29, 1981
Young Offenders Act
between provinces and territories in different methods applied to bring about the process with young people being treated differently, depending upon where they reside or, perhaps, where the offence is committed.
Although the diversion provisions are worthy of general support, the process by which diversion is achieved is definitely in need of further examination by the committee. How will the changes be paid for? Who will be responsible for funding? Again, the absence of a commitment to provide financial support for the costly screening process is of great concern. The effect of section 4 can only be as good as its implementation and, to be sure, the provinces and territories will, I expect, be resisting picking up the tab, as it were. As the Canadian Corrections Association has already pointed out, merely changing the legislation without improving the range and quality of resources is an exercise in futility. But that is what is being attempted here, and I would hope that the standing committee, when seized of the legislation, will clean up what appears to be a very serious omission.
The next area of the legislation which I would like to touch briefly upon is that which concerns itself with detention and bail. The legislation would require youths to be detained separately from adults. If no place for detention for young people exists in the area, however, the youth could be placed in a building housing adult offenders. In my opinion this is simply not acceptable. Young people dealt with under this legislation should be assiduously kept apart from adult offenders. Once again the government has failed to offer funds for the additional youth detention buildings which ought to be provided for and which ought to be a requirement under the legislation.
The bill provides that a youth can avoid incarceration or detention in an institution if he or she is placed in the care of a responsible person who is "willing and able to take care of and exercise control over a young person who has been arrested". This may be found in subsection (4) of clause 7 of the bill before us. The young person must also be willing to go with the person in whose care he or she is discharged. This is a proposal which was supported by our government and which is worthy of continued support. It provided, as it does now, a positive alternative to incarceration where parents or a responsible adult may step in and assume responsibility for the young person.
One important change in the new, as opposed to the old, legislation is the new requirement that notice to the parents of the accused must be given if a young person is arrested and detained. Under the old legislation the state acquired the position of parens patriae and parents or guardians were often uninformed as to their child's circumstances. In the new legislation there is provision for direct participation of the parents in all aspects of the process under this bill.
The requirement of notice applies not only to an occasion where a child has been detained, but also to cases where an appearance notice or summons has been issued, as well as when a youth is released giving his promise to appear, or is released on a recognizance. Such notice requirements are
welcome in the face of total absence of such protections in the existing legislation. It ensures that the rights and responsibilities of parents are maintained up to the maximum age of jurisdiction. Entitlement for bail will also change to the same as for adult offenders and will be governed by the provisions of the Criminal Code.
The next aspect of the bill with which I would like to deal is the right of the young person to assistance and representation. The Juvenile Delinquents Act is silent on the matter of a young person's right to counsel. The bill before us states expressly in clause 11 that a young person is entitled to be assisted by a lawyer during all proceedings. In the notice sent to a parent immediately upon arrest or issuance of an appearance notice, summons or recognizance, a statement of the right to retain counsel must be included. The judge is required to inform the youth of his or her right to be represented by counsel when the accused appears before a court. If counsel has not already been retained, an opportunity will be given to retain one.
In my submission the new legislation does not go far enough. Although the right to counsel is expressly given in the bill- and I would draw this point to the attention of the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan), if he would follow me for a moment or two-in my view there is a very serious omission. It allows for an adult to assist a young person but it does not guarantee the young person the right to counsel. The role of a lawyer is vital in judicial proceedings. He or she must ensure that the youth receives a full and fair hearing in the matter of adjudicating the facts upon which the charge is based, and that the disposition of the case is, in fact, in the best interests of the child.
As a counsellor to the youth, the lawyer can discover the limitations and services offered by the court and should check and challenge the modes of disposition presented to the court. In short, the lawyer's function is to act as a check on the authorities, to question and challenge disposition proposals and therapy, even to the extent of determining the validity of the very base on which proposals are made. The fears of those who believe the lawyer's presence will lead to a formal, legal loophole-ridden and technical atmosphere are groundless, in my submission. With trained lawyers on both sides the operation of the entire procedure would run more smoothly. Formalism could help to rid the system of possible abuses. A youth is entitled to protection from well-intended but misguided coercion.
An interesting provision in this bill, and one which is worthy of support, relates to the issue which I have just been discussing. Although the role of a parent is very important, it is recognized that the parental influence is not always in the best interests of a young person. Many parents cannot afford a lawyer, nor can they take the time off to appear at the court hearing. Time and time again I have seen it happen in juvenile court, where the youth is there without parent and without representation. If the parent does not appear on the youth's behalf, he is often overwhelmed and overawed by the courtroom atmosphere. The easiest course of action for the parent is quiet acquiescence in the advice of police officers, well-inten-
May 29, 1981

tioned advice I am sure, or probation officers. In my observation, the best interests of the child have not always been served.
Clause 11, subclause (7), states that where the interests of the youth and parent are in conflict, or where the best interests of the youth are not being served, the court:
-shall ensure that the young person is represented by counsel independent of his parents.
That provision is there but it does not plug the loophole that I brought to the minister's attention a moment ago. A case should not have to be made for legal representation of children charged with offences. Provision for legal aid would help to alleviate the inequities in the present system which tends to discriminate unfairly against native children and against the poor.
The next issue in this bill deals with transfer to the adult court. The bill allows for a transfer only if the youth committed the offence when he was 14 years of age or older. There are explicit criteria provided to guide a judge's decision which is lacking in the old legislation. For instance, the judge must consider a number of factors, such as the predisposition report, which is mandatory, the age and the background of the offender, and the seriousness of the alleged offence. The judge must also consider the parents' representations before making a transfer order. The transfer order itself is subject to appeal. This is another area which requires much closer scrutiny at the committee stage; in particular, the criteria that judges must consider in making a transfer order. The rights and interests of the young offender as well as the rights of society must be properly protected. The committee will have to tackle this problem, I suppose, by calling appropriate witnesses and reexamining this whole area of the bill far more carefully.
Now 1 would like to refer to the matter of disposition, and that is, sentencing powers. There is a much wider variety of options available to the courts as compared with the old act. The provisions are identical to the 1979 proposals which our government brought in. There is one exception to that, and that is that a combination of the options can now be used so long as they do not exceed two years in total. Options available include an absolute discharge, a fine of up to $1,000, a restitution or compensation order, a community service order, compensation by personal service, probation of up to two years, custody of up to two years, or any other reasonable and ancillary condition that the court deems advisable and in the best interests of the young person and society. These changes are consistent with the philosophy underlying the bill before us as stated by the Solicitor General and I will not repeat those statements. They are to be found in his remarks on the proposed legislation in this place on April 15 last.
This philosophy is reflected throughout the legislation. For example, an important feature of the bill is the abolition of what the old legislation describes as a delinquency. Under the new legislation, a young person would only be held responsible for offences under the Criminal Code and other federal stat-
Young Offenders Act
utes and regulations. The so-called status offences will be no more. This reflects the constitutional division of responsibility between the federal and the provincial and territorial levels, as well as approving the practice in many jurisdictions of decriminalizing behaviour which is no longer seen as serious enough to rationalize its inclusion under criminal law.
The provisions for disposition also reflect this basic philosophy. They recognize the rights of the young person to be equal to those of an adult. Maximum sentences, for the first time, are established. In making the disposition, the judge must consider the type of offence committed, the predisposition report, and any other relevant information. In the Juvenile Delinquents Act, reference to "the child's own good and the best interest of the community", is absent, which allows the court to move away from its parens patriae role and focus its intention on its role as a court. Although the parental role still exists, its importance is diminished and it cannot be used for excessive intervention. Another protection against abuse is the requirement in clause 20, subclause (5), that the judge provide written reasons for the disposition.
The two-year maximum of disposition orders is a change from the 1975 report, as well as the 1977 proposals of the Solicitor General which recommended a maximum of three years. This is a very positive change and reflects, in my view, the past experience of those involved in this area, that two years is sufficient to meet the needs of young people.
A criticism of the disposition order deals with the concept of community service and restitution as being preferable to orders based on punishment. Although it is a step in the right direction and certainly worthy of support, there should be some provision to ensure compliance. For example, the rules governing custody are quite explicit. The same thought and foresight ought to be applied to restitution orders. The legislation is breaking into virgin territory with these new concepts. Though it is recognized that, as such, not all difficulties are foreseeable, it does not take a great amount of foresight, for instance, to realize that there will be occasions, when a young person will not comply with his or her restitution order, or when a diversion program will not work. So, what happens then? Bill C-61 appears to be silent on this most important point, in my submission, and this aspect of the bill will certainly require discussion at the committee stage.
In my submission, as a finality to this point, the existing provisions in the bill are vague and the checks and balances so necessary are simply not present. The bill provides for mandatory disposition orders. Under the old act there was no mandatory review process, and power was given to the judge, in any case, to have a youth brought back to court before he reached the age of 21 without any specific reason. The judge had the power, which was virtually unchecked, to impose any disposition in substitution for the original one.
The important new provision for mandatory review will ensure, in my view, that the welfare and progress of a youth will be subject to continuing review from the beginning to the end of the disposition. Where custody is ordered, there is a yearly mandatory review which can occur more frequently on

May 29, 1981
Young Offenders Act
application of the young person, the provincial or territorial director, the parents or the Crown. The review can be conducted by the court or a provincially or territorially appointed review board. But if the review relates to the basic nature of a custodial sentence, then only the youth court would have jurisdiction. Upon completion of a review, a judge may reduce the disposition to any lesser one provided for under the act, including discharge. If it is found that a youth deliberately failed to comply with the original disposition, then the court itself can raise the disposition.
The important changes to note here are, first, the availability of review and the youth's knowledge and presence at that review; and second, that open-ended dispositions are no longer permitted.
Criticisms of these sections of the bill relate primarily not to the way the review boards will be functioning so much as to their composition. The boards will fall under the jurisdiction of the provinces and territories and there are no guidelines set out for the provinces and territories to follow in making appointments to them. This gives me grave cause for concern, as it should every member. As there are no requirements for qualifications for membership of the review board it is conceivable, indeed, it is quite to be expected, that it would be comprised of political appointees or persons unqualified for the sensitive job that is required, especially a board that is dealing exclusively with young people. In my submission the board must be competent and without bias in order to function properly and effectively. The board's composition should consist of individuals who have some sympathy with the problems of young people and some degree of expertise in their approach to how the problems will be dealt with and solved. This is usually the last criteria found in political appointments.
It is all very well in a body such as the National Parole Board to let political persuasion be a criteria in the selection process, but it is totally out of place in the appointment of individuals who comprise a review board dealing with young people. It would be my strong submission, therefore, that when the matter is considered by committee, some guidelines as to the qualifications of those who will be sitting on these review boards should be considered and, it is hoped, will be spelled out by amendments in the bill.
Another aspect of the bill deals with the appeal process. This is one of the most welcome changes to be found in the new bill. Under the existing legislation, clause 37 provides for an appeal which is allowed "from any decision" but only with "special leave from a Supreme Court judge". Before leave can be granted, the judge must consider that to do so is "essential to the public interest or for the due administration of justice."
Because of the wording of the statute, appeals have been kept to a minimum, which was the apparent intention of the language then used. The present procedure does not provide additional protection for young offenders, but rather it restricts the right of appeal.
This bill gives youths the same right of appeal as adults under the Criminal Code. The ambiguities and balancing problems inherent in the wording of the Juvenile Delinquents Act are dispensed with. The appeal procedure in the Code is clear and well established so it is with a great deal of approval that we greet this provision in the legislation. It will certainly alleviate the potential abuses of and infringements upon the basic rights of young people that have in the past consistently occurred.
Other aspects of this bill which are dealt with are fingerprinting and photographing of young persons. The bill permits fingerprinting and photographing, but if the young person is acquitted or proceedings are discontinued, the prints and photographs must be destroyed. The practice to be followed is that set out in the Identification of Criminals Act. There are also special provisions in respect of storage of these kinds of records. Generally speaking, the new provisions will be helpful in clarifying a situation which is unclear at present.
With regard to court records under this bill, once a sentence is completed and a qualifying period without crime is completed then the records are destroyed. The qualifying period is two years for a summary offence, five years for an indictable offence.
Under the existing Juvenile Delinquents Act there are no provisions regarding the destruction of records, nor are there controls for the creation and maintenance of confidentiality and accessibility of juvenile court records. The new provisions, in my submission, are to be supported because they allow a young person to enter adulthood with a clean slate. Under the present legislation a youth would be labelled a delinquent for the rest of his life.
Having addressed the matter point by point, I want to say, in terminating these remarks, that the provisions of the bill with respect to trial proceedings being held in camera are a welcome change. Under the present act, the trial proceedings were held in camera. The philosophy underlying this was that trials involving children should be without publicity and should be held apart from trials of adults. We can certainly agree with the latter point. In camera hearings are and should be viewed with suspicion always, as they are always subject to potential abuse. The press cannot act, for example, as a check on arbitrary court action.
The new bill allows hearings to be open to the public but restrictions will remain. The judge may exclude people in the interest of public morals, administration of justice or where the information being presented to the court would be seriously prejudicial or injurious to any youth present-either the accused, the victim, or a witness. The provisions with respect to the publication of information are also to be welcomed.
Having gone through the measure seriatim, Mr. Speaker, I would hope that the record of today's proceedings would commend itself to those members of the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs and that they will study the suggestions I have made with great interest and attention. I hope all the points that I have covered will come back to the House in the form of an improved piece of legislation.
May 29, 1981
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I have some advantages speaking on this bill and I have some disadvantages. My advantage is that I am not a lawyer but I am a parent. I have raised five children through this difficult period. My disadvantage in the House, as I speak on the Young Offenders Act, is also that I am not a lawyer.
This is an important and complex piece of legislation. It is, as my hon. colleague and neighbour from Durham-Northumb-erland (Mr. Lawrence) pointed out earlier this month, the first major social justice bill to come before this House in over three decades. I think it is a sad thing to have waited so long for the reforms necessary in dealing with young offenders in this country. It is sad that the government has waited so long before giving this major issue the priority it deserves. Swept to power 13 years ago by promising Canadians a "just society", it is only now that the government takes serious steps.
What are the reforms that the government is proposing? I am pleased to see-except for one or two points which I will deal with later-that the government is stealing the proposals put forward by the solicitor general of the 1979 Progressive Conservative government. It is pleasing to see the Liberal government recognizing that good ideas on social justice come from the Conservative party. Perhaps it could also accept some of our good ideas on economics.
What has taken place in Canada with respect to juvenile delinquency under our Liberal administration? From 1974 to 1978 violent juvenile delinquency increased by 60 per cent. I am not going to blame this on any particular government. We have seen in the last decade increased violent crime in all age groups in North America. But I would like to make the point to hon. members that problems of this nature are problems for society as a whole and, to a great extent, reflect the problems of our society.
The tragedy of violent juvenile crime is not going to be stopped simply by passing an updated piece of legislation which should have been passed ten years ago. Our problems are much more fundamental than the important, but nevertheless, non-crucial, issues of administration and mechanisms of our young justice system.
What governments must begin to address is the increasing casualness and decreasing morality of our society. I know that it is not fashionable to speak of morality, but morality is necessary. If the word "morality" is too offensive for some of my colleague in the left-wing of this House, or too religious for others, I shall not apologize but instead substitute the word "ethics".
The concept of responsibility must be reintroduced into our society, not just with respect to the actions of young offenders but with respect to all Canadians. We must climb out of the ethical cesspool that we have been in and have built for ourselves which permits the individual all too frequently to blame the consequences of his actions and circumstances on
Young Offenders Act
other people, particularly on government, which they expect will do all for everyone.
Accountability must be introduced to our society. We must stamp out the fraudulent notion that someone or something, whether it be big government or big brother, is always going to solve our problems for us. Mistakes are always going to be made by individuals in our society, and mistakes should be judged with compassion. But there is a turning point, a point where too much compassion becomes cruelty. It is an unintended cruelty to be sure, but it is no less harsh. There is a point where too much sympathy, when handing out consequences for an individual's actions, can begin to encourage the individual to continue making mistakes, a point where the individual is not appropriately aware of the seriousness of his mistakes, a point where the individual begins to expect, and begins to take for granted that someone else, not him, is responsible.
This point, I feel, is passed in the Young Offenders Act before us. I would urge members, especially members of my own party, should the government force this bill to committee, to review carefully the provision in the bill which would remove the concept of the liability of parents for criminal acts committed by their young people. This concept, present in Section 22 of the Juvenile Delinquents Act, has been removed and replaced with the view that only the young people themselves are financially responsible for their acts.
On this point, having raised five children above this age myself, I feel there must be consequences for their actions which must be dealt with in the home. The matter cannot be dealt with only in the courts. I plead with members of my own party to put this provision, presently in Section 22, into this bill.
The phrase "young people" is sometimes misleading. Let me emphasize that we are talking about children, those who have just left babyhood. The point I am making, is that we are talking about children who have not received the proper discipline. We are talking about children who have not received proper upbringing or who have not had the moral values instilled into them, as I mentioned earlier. I believe it is the moral fibre of this country which is at fault and causing these children to do these things. Parents or guardians must have the incentive to stop their children from doing wrong. Parents or guardians must have the incentive to develop some responsibility in their children. I am speaking of "their" children; they are not our children but the children of the parents. The failure to include an equivalent of Section 22 in this bill may well add to the decay of the morality of our society.
I believe it is insulting for this House to presume to speak of giving parents incentives, but let's face it, there are some bad parents in this country. At times I could include myself in that group. The courts should set an example of morality but the courts should not be the only ones to do this. Parents must also set such standards. I firmly believe that possible parental liability for the criminal actions of children will help to encourage the setting of these standards.

May 29, 1981
Young Offenders Act
1 mentioned that I am at a disadvantage because I am not a lawyer. Other than my philosophical worry, there are two technical aspects of this bill about which I am worried. The first was well presented on May 12 by the hon. member for Durham-Northumberland, who is a lawyer and someone I trust in these matters. I know that the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) was not in the House at that time nor is he in the House now, which is a shame, because the hon. member made some good points on this matter. One in particular has to do with the lack of uniformity across Canada of a maximum age defining a young person. For that reason,' I trust that this amendment will be adopted.
I think it very important that the administration of justice for young people not be tackled in a piecemeal approach, varying from one province to another. A 16-year-old in one province is the same as a 16-year-old in another province and should not be treated as more mature, more responsible, than an 18-year-old whether in the same province or in another province.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Does that line of reasoning not apply to the charter of rights?

Contrary to the Liberal position.
My other technical concern is with clause 11, subclause (1), on the right to "retain and instruct" counsel, and with subclause (4) of the same clause respecting legal aid. I would ask other members in this House, those more familiar with the law, to look at these provisions closely should the government force the bill to committee. I am worried that the act does not take sufficient precautions in making certain that another huge and costly extension is not added to our present legal aid bureaucracy.
I would like to reiterate my point that I am worried for the young people of this country because in some cases both parents have had to go to work, partly as a result of inflation. I am concerned they are not getting direction. I am concerned, too, that there is no morality in their society. When I was a young person I was taken to church on Sunday. I was brought up with some morality and when I committed an offence, no matter how minor it was, my father dealt with me in the way he thought appropriate. It hurt. I did not like it but I respected it. I do not necessarily follow that philosophy today because our own morality has fallen apart.
I plead with this House and with the members serving on this committee to look at this bill very carefully to make certain that they deal with all factors, not just the legal factors. Because our young people are the citizens of this country who will eventually be governing Canada.
Hear, hear!

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Kaplan that Bill C-61, respecting young offenders and to repeal the Juvenile Deliquents Act, be read the second time
May 29, 1981
and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Lawrence (p. 9497).

Mr. Speaker, this is a bit of an historic moment for me. Although I have had many occasions to speak in this House, this is the first time I have done so without there being one cabinet minister present-not that it will make any great difference.
There are a lot of former ones though.
It will be a rather interesting Friday afternoon with no minister of the Crown in the House.
There are a few hopefuls.

This young offenders legislation needs to be updated as there has been very little change made to it since it was introduced in 1908. It is important that we look at our young people and reflect upon the way we impose the law on that sector of society and make the necessary changes to both the writing and administration of it.
Although this legislation is basically good, there are some inequities which, with the agreement of the various parties in committee, could be done away with to make it a better piece of legislation. I want to reflect on the subject of young people and why it is timely that we bring about some changes to this legislation.
Those who watch the charts and graphs on the rate of crime in Canada in particular and in North America in general have noted a continual increase. An hon. member opposite shakes his head, indicating that this is not the case. I do not know what data he has looked at which indicate there is less crime today per capita than in former years. There are very few people who would believe that crime has decreased in North America.
I believe the legislation is important because I think the tendency toward crime will increase. That tendency will increase because of the advent of the silicon chip in this electronic age. The use of technology will take meaningful employment away from larger percentages of our society. That will cause frustration among our population and the crime rate will increase. Thirty, forty or fifty years ago and beyond there was meaningful employment for people who had low skill levels or intelligence levels. Such people would have difficulty finding employment today. One or two generations ago a person with an IQ of 80 or 90 could always clean out livery stables. Snow had to be shovelled. Such work is now done by machinery. Mechanization, electroncis and superelectronics will, in the not too distant future, make it very difficult for a large part of our population to find employment. That phenomenon raises an interesting question respecting law and order and how to handle young people.
If I might digress from that point, I want to address myself for a few minutes to the North American phenomenon of
Young Offenders Act
adolescence. I believe adolescence has been created largely in Canada, the United States and the industrial nations of northern Europe and that in most countries of the world there is no adolescence. Psychologists have delved into the matter of the stress brought about by the change from childhood to adulthood. They have studied the stress among young people undergoing what is called adolescent change. They travelled to some of the lesser developed nations to find out why the change from childhood to adulthood causes stress, but in those lesser developed countries that change takes place almost overnight. In some of those countries two weeks after pubic rites people are no longer children. They go on hunting trips with their fathers, live under the rules and assume the responsibilities of adulthood. The interesting thing this team of psychologists found is that in lesser developed countries there is virtually no stress involved. Adolescents in North America are in limbo. They are not given appropriate responsibilities.
In our recent debates on the Constitution and when people appeared before the committee studying the Constitution the words often used in the committee and in this House were "my rights". We discussed the rights of women, the rights of children, the rights of Indians or native peoples and the rights of the handicapped. The legislation before us deals with the rights of youth, but I submit that this legislation is void of an adequate discussion of responsibility.
In dealing with the phenomenon of adolescence in industrial nations I remind hon. members that this country was settled by people who involved themselves in some phenomenal activities. The achievements of those people would hardly be believable today. Before he was 21 Lord Strathcona was making moves to set himself up in some very significant business enterprises. Ezra Eddy set up the E. B. Eddy Company. At the age of 15 he was very much an independent businessman. Sir John A. Macdonald articled in law at the age of 16.
Part of the reason for our youth crime rate is that we have talked much about rights, but we have not created a climate which would allow adolescents to pattern their behaviour in such a way as to excercise their full responsibilities. If we look around the world and also consider our own earlier history, we can demonstrate that the assuming of adult responsibility is something which the majority of our so-called adolescents can do. If they were rewarded appropriately for responsible behaviour, we could have a much more mature society.
On a congratulatory note, the first comment I want to make about this bill is that it is appropriate that it should encourage adolescents to assume more of the responsibilities of adulthood. My criticism is that I do not believe the bill goes far enough. For example, I believe that the concept of retribution might well be followed with respect to youth. A youth involved in a misdemeanour or a crime should repay the debt he owes to society and to the person or persons against whom he has committed his crime.
Too often today we let youths and adults get off with mere fines or prison terms. In many respects that is an easy way of removing the sense of obligation which should follow a criminal act. I see no reason why offenders, both youth and adult,

May 29, 1981
Young Offenders Act
should not repay their debt and perhaps repay more than the dollar value of that debt. Offenders could do such things as cleaning up a mile of highway or several miles of highway. There should be some public service performed in order to demonstrate the need to accept responsibility beyond just the paying of a fine, which at present can be paid by a parent or even by a child, if he happens to have money. Offenders should not be required simply to pay money and then be excused. People should be required to behave in a certain manner. They should be required to pay for their misbehaviour.
There should be some differentiation between crimes committed by adolescents as a result of an association with other adolescents and crimes committed as a result of the influence of adults. There should be a differentiation when an adult uses a child to commit crime, for pornography, for prostitution or for any other crime, whether it be organized or otherwise. In such cases there should be much harsher penalties for the adults involved. It may be presumed that the youth involved is of an immature mental age and that, while the youth will have to bear his responsibility, the full wrath of the law of the land should fall upon the adult.
There are areas of this bill in which I think some improvement can be made. First of all, it is my opinion that the title, the Young Offenders Act, is better than referring to juvenile delinquents because I think there is a negative connotation to those words. And with respect to the option many of these youths will have for an in camera hearing, it is my position that, while it will in some cases save the individuals some embarrassment, I do not believe that the due process of law is necessarily protected in that situation in a country that believes in freedom of the press and information. To allow a segment of our society called "youth" to have the protection of in camera proceedings has as much, if not more, opportunity for abuse as it does for service. I am nervous and concerned about this clause because, while it might be more acceptable for certain testimony, to have an entire case heard in camera is, I believe, a dangerous precedent in Canada where we simply do not believe in closed courts. The courts should be open, and if we are to expect a higher degree of responsibility from young people and we are going to treat them in a more responsible adult way, then I think an in camera proceeding is not the appropriate way to achieve that.
Another aspect on which I would like to comment is that of the juvenile review board. Here we have a proposal to establish a review board across Canada but with no guidelines as to who should sit on that board. That opens the floodgates for political appointments, appointments of people who may or may not be in a position to serve with the kind of expertise that we need on a board of that kind.
In addition to that, I believe it would be appropriate and beneficial to the young people concerned if we had assurances that a number of young people sat on that board along with the appropriate proportion of adults. This has been tried in other countries, including the United States, and been found to
have some considerable effect on their peers. In many cases a youth appearing before his peers has more respect for the law thereafter than he would if direction were coming from an authoritarian adult figure.
In summary, Mr. Speaker, it would be my view that we ought not to let this legislation pass without specifically stipulating what the guidelines should be for the review board, and that at least some members of that board should be senior youth carefully selected for their ability to consider the crime involved and whether or not parole should be granted.
Another aspect of this bill which ought to be improved at the committee stage is with respect to the definition by age of a young person. The age of majority in many provinces of Canada is 18, but it is not universal. In some provinces it can be as low as 16, and in others 17 or 19.
This is a good piece of legislation, timely and probably long overdue, but I think it would be of considerable benefit to Canada if the age limit were universal across the country. Whether you live in British Columbia, Prince Edward Island, Ontario or Quebec, or one of the territories, is irrelevant. It is my view that the Young Offenders Act, so far as age is concerned, should be standardized across Canada, even if it means further negotiations with the provinces between now and the final reading to reach an agreement on that.
Another aspect I should like to speak to is that the Young Offenders Act provides that young offenders would serve their sentences in the same institutions as presently house adult offenders. While this may seem contradictory to my earlier comments concerning young people accepting the full responsibilities of adulthood, I am not of the opinion that you can put a young person in an institution which houses adults whose behaviour has been judged by society as negative.
I think it important that the federal government provide the financing for the setting up, where necessary, of institutions for youthful offenders, thereby keeping them away from the hardened criminals who occupy these adult institutions. I cannot think of a better way to teach young people about crime than to lock them away with hardened adult criminals. If this legislation is not changed in this respect, then I think it is certainly a retrograde step in our treatment of the young offender.
Another aspect of this bill is the wording which indicates that the younger person may have counsel, a right which is different from an adult's right to counsel. If we are to treat young people in a more responsible manner, which is the objective of this bill, I believe they should have the guarantee of counsel in the same way as any adult who allegedly committed a crime would be guaranteed that right. The simple provision that he may have counsel is unsatisfactory and is not strong enough in its wording. In its review, the committee should take a look at that matter to ensure that youths are guaranteed the full right to counsel in the same manner as adults, although they are younger than 18 years of age.

Historically our approach to law and order has been a punitive one, followed more recently by the protection of society and, even more recently, the talk of rehabilitation. In terms of the old law and order system, the punitive approach was to draw and quarter. Punishing people for the sole purpose of punishment should have no place in any system of law and order.
With respect to the protection of society and rehabilitation, I believe when a criminal has affronted society that the first objective ought to be the protection of society. But 1 would change my belief in that regard and say that the first objective with young offenders ought to be rehabilitation. Also I believe rehabilitation ought to be a part of adult programs, but in that case the protection of society ought to be the dominant objective. Rehabilitation ought to be the dominant objective when dealing with young people. We must be able to get them started, reward them for their capabilities and recognize that people, whether they be young or old, male or female, or however they are classified or stratified by society, can end up in criminal situations for reasons which do not necessarily demonstrate a calculated mental process in terms of their decision to commit a crime.
If that sounds like a lot of mush, let me repeat it by indicating that there are associated factors in our daily living patterns which have been linked to criminal activities. For example, the diets and eating patterns of North Americans is one of them. I know my following comments will not be part of the bill or an amendment to the legislation, but I encourage members of Parliament to use their influence in an attempt to rid school cafeterias of junk foods. I know we will not legislate it, but at the present time there is an overwhelming amount of information in that regard.
I hear some chuckles from the other side. Perhaps they have not read this well-researched information. Some examples are the overuse of sugar, pop and junk foods, the tensions and stresses inherent in people, the lack of appropriate vitamins and minerals in diets. I know it is difficult to excuse people's behaviour because they did not eat correctly, but it is our obligation in our role of giving leadership to talk whenever possible about the importance of these factors and their effect upon the behaviour of individuals, be they youths or adults.
As I indicated earlier, another factor is the area of jobs. With the advance of electronics, silicon chips and expensive computerization, it is incumbent upon us to remember that it is not good enough for people to be provided with goods, services and an adequate standard of living in terms of food, clothing and housing. Every human being thirsts to become a meaningful participant in society. He wants to "feel like a somebody", that he can do something; he wants a feeling of some personal worth and that he matters or counts. The removal of jobs from large sectors of society will increase the crime rate. If one does not feel meaningful and have some sense of self-respect, one will seek attention by practising disrespect. People by their nature must be noticed. If vast numbers of jobs are to be removed by electronics, they must be
Young Offenders Act
replaced with opportunities for people to feel that they are achievers in some other dimension.
I think I have covered all my points. I am sure further discussions will take place at committee stage. We require a tightening up of the language and words in the bill before us. There must be a reflection of the philosophy we want with respect to law and order. I do not believe there is a great disagreement among party members as to the principal objectives of this bill. Hopefully some minor alterations can be made in committee, so that in 1981 we will have a piece of legislation which is more contemporary than that with which we are living at present. Essentially it is the original 1908 legislation. Very few amendments have taken place in the interim, but obviously there has been an enormous change in our social behaviour in that same interim. I hope this legislation will receive the benefit of some good amendments before it comes before the House for third reading.

Mr. Speaker, let me begin by sharing with the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Malone) what a delight it is to follow him in the House. Many times I have had the occasion to hear him speak in the chamber. He has not only made good sense, but his speeches make good reading.
During the course of my remarks dealing with the proposed Young Offenders Act, I plan to refer to a number of letters I have received from students throughout my constituency. Most of us on occasion have opportunities to speak with school groups and the students of our constituencies. Prior to this legislation being introduced, I had an opportunity to speak to a number of classes. I asked them for the benefit of their input. I have approximately a dozen letters. I will not read them all, but I would like to point out some of their highlights.
It is important to instil, in not only our students but in the entire population, the fact that views and concerns of individuals who are not members of Parliament are brought forward in the chamber. It is important to practise participatory democracy.
This bill is very similar to the one which we introduced in the short period of time when our party formed the government. Our party supports the legislation which is before us. We have moved an amendment to it which, if passed, would provide some consistency to the maximum age, which is something I will deal with later. I find it most appropriate that I am able to refer to specific correspondence I have received, since far too often as far as our student population is concerned, our young adult population, the publicity they receive is negative. Most of our young people are individuals of whom we can be truly proud.
I am able to illustrate this by reading into the record a number of letters I have received. I would like to do this so that the individuals who have sent me these letters will be aware that their thoughts are being considered in this chamber. The first letter I wish to refer to is from Jeff Plantje. He

Another letter I received was from Wes Marko who supports, in general, the legislation before us.
Karen Kartz wrote to me to point out that it would be beneficial to have juveniles detained in separate quarters from adults. She disagrees with youths being photographed and fingerprinted. Under the legislation before us, in the event that an individual is acquitted, the photographs and fingerprints will be immediately destroyed. After a period of two years for summary conviction offences, if the offender commits no further crime, and after a period of five years in the case of indictable offences, the records will be destroyed.
Another letter I would mention is from Colleen Ropser, who indicates her feelings that members of Parliament and of the legislatures should be aware that young people do require a certain amount of discipline. But, more than discipline, she feels they require guidance.

The final letter I have here is from Andrew Singh. I will not refer to any of the specifics contained in it, but I would like to underscore the contribution he made in the discussions we had at the Salisbury Composite High School. I must say that I was encouraged to see young people such as those who wrote to me interested in our legislative process. I was pleased to see they took time out of their busy schedules to correspond with me and express their concerns with respect to this legislation.
As I indicated earlier, Mr. Speaker, this legislation was not before the House at the time I spoke with these students. I forwarded to them copies of the bill. All of us in this chamber can applaud the young people of our society throughout Canada for the responsible manner in which they approach many of the frustrating decisions which they must make in this day and age.
As a father or three sons aged 14, 12 and eight, I realize some of the difficulties which our young people face. While this piece of legislation seems to deal with a narrow subject, in reality it deals with a much broader topic. Young people of today must deal with values, family life and the moral fibre of society.
As my colleague the hon. member for Crowfoot stated earlier, some of the statistics which are before us are very worrisome. When we look at the figures we find that there has been an increase of some 60 per cent in violent juvenile delinquency from 1974 to 1978. Most shocking of all is the increase in violence by young people against themselves. In the past decade the suicide rate for young people aged 15 to 19 years of age has increased some 59 per cent. These are just a few of the reasons for the need to take a good, hard look at the best way for society to respond to young people and their needs.
If we are to be serious about the problems faced by young people who come into conflict with the law, we must collectively look at such issues as child abuse, our divorce rate, the reasons for teenage suicide, the relationship between crime and the criminal in the early years of development and the over-all mental health picture of our young people. All Conservatives!

One of the reasons 1 thought I might get to my feet for a few minutes on this Friday afternoon is, I admit, a personal one. Quite a few hon. members have referred to this act as having been passed in 1908. Of course, to most hon. members, that is a year which is a long time ago.
Stanley remembers it!
You were here!
Was it long in committee?

I was not here. At least, I was not present in this chamber. Of course, this chamber was not here; it was another building in those days. However, this did prompt me to go into the library and look up the Hansard of 1908, and I found one or two things which, to me, were quite interesting.
I have known for a number of years and I have recounted several times, that on the day I was born, June 18, 1908, this House debated and passed the first piece of legislation providing anything in the way of pensions for the general public. It was the Government Annuities Act, so I suppose there is some connection between the fact that on the day I was born that bill was passed.
What did this House do the next day, June 19, Mr. Speaker when, no doubt, this House had learned that I had arrived in this world? It gave first reading to the Juvenile Delinquents Act. I am sure I must have complained and howled about it but I suppose if I see some meaning in the Government Annuities Act being passed on the day I was born, I have to admit that there could be some meaning in the Juvenile Delinquents Act being given first reading the very next day!
Then my interest led me to turn to the pages of Hansard and consult the index to see what I could learn about the debate on the bill. It took place on July 8, 1908. That was the entire debate as far as this House was concerned. There was no debate on second reading, and no debate on third reading. All of the debate took place in committee of the whole. Of course, members complained then, as they do now, about its being rushed through. But even those who complained about its being rushed through did not try to stop it.
The entire debate on the Juvenile Delinquents Act in 1908 covers four or five pages of Hansard. The printing in 1908 was a little smaller than it is now, but at best that is less than an hour's time given to this Juvenile Delinquents Act of 1908. Mind you, it had been debated in the Senate first and came to this House as a Senate bill. One or two kindred souls of mine were on the floor that day and complained about its being dealt with in the Senate first and asked why this House should be expected to pass the bill in a hurry just because the Senate had sent it to this House saying that this is the important House. That was a good thing to be said back in 1908, as it still is.
The debate was also interesting in that some of the things being said today were said then. The defence of the bill on the government side, which was Liberal, as it has been for most of this century-it is time for a change-was to the effect that it was time to remove our little "boys and girls", as one member referred to them, from legislation such as the Criminal Code. It was an attempt to find a way to provide for more rehabilitation and to give our little boys and girls, or young children, a chance.
The Tories from the other side did not like its being rushed through. It certainly was rushed through because it was done in an hour. We have spent four days on second reading! Things change but they do not change that much, do they?
The argument of the opponents on the Tory side of the House, was that it was unfair to boys and girls to make them the subject of special legislation; after all, if they were old enough to commit crime, they should be covered the same as ordinary criminals but that for the most part, children were the responsibility of their parents.
I am not quoting from the debate of the last three of four days, Mr. Speaker. I am referring to things that were said in this House 73 years ago this July 8. I throw that in for a bit of Friday afternoon interest.
I certainly express the view that I am sure all of us agree with, that regardless of what happens to human beings who are around for 73 years, certainly a piece of legislation that has been around that long needs to be reviewed and recast. I hope that as a result of this debate on second reading and the detailed consideration that will take place in committee, we will come up with a piece of legislation in 1981 that will be an advance on what was passed the summer I was born.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, it is always a pleasure to follow the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). When I knew I was going to have to say a few words on the Young Offenders Act, I, too, checked with the Library of Parliament on the evolution of the Juvenile Delinquents Act.
My hon. friend spoke about 1908. I noticed that the first legislation adopted in relation to young offenders in Canada was the Act for More Speedy Trial and Punishment of Juve-
May 29, 1981

nile Offenders, enacted in 1867. I thought our hon. friend might have been there around that time.
Speak for yourself.

I am sorry; I forget it was in 1908 that the hon. member was born.
This enactment as well as legislation adopted in 1869 and 1886, was incorporated into the first Criminal Code passed by Parliament in 1892. These provisions ensured that the trial of young person under the age of 16 years took place apart from that of adults charged with criminal offences. Once convicted, a young person was to be detained in prison separate from adult criminals.
A comprehensive statute dealing with young offenders was not enacted until 1908 when the Juvenile Delinquents Act was adopted by Parliament. It was passed as the result of a concerted campaign by several child care workers and magistrates who were inspired by the youth court movement in the United States and the social reform ideas which were in vogue at that time. The act was adopted at the end of a parliamentary session after a relatively short debate.
In 1929-the year after I was born-Parliament consolidated the act by re-enacting the 1908 version with the amendments effected to it in 1912, 1914, 1921 and 1924. This consolidation occurred as the result of a federal-provincial conference on the revision of the juvenile delinquents act, held in 1928 in Ottawa under the sponsorship of the then minister of justice, Ernest Lapointe, the Canadian Council on Child Welfare and the Canadian Conference of Child Protection Officers.
Despite minor technical amendments to the Juvenile Delinquents Act by Parliament in 1932, 1935, 1936, 1947, 1949, 1951, 1972, and 1979, it is for all intents and purposes the same statute as that adopted in 1929.
That is a little bit of history. I think my constituents would like to know exactly what has been happening and why we are debating this Young Offenders Act today.
Over the past several years a number of publications and reports have been issued by the federal government addressing the problem of juvenile delinquency in Canada, particularly the inadequacy of the present law for dealing with this problem.
Despite the proliferation of documents citing both the desirability and need to update current juvenile law and recommending various proposals to bring about this long called for reform, such a goal has yet to be achieved.
The Solicitor General of Canada (Mr. Kaplan) considers the revision of Canadian juvenile law as a matter deserving urgent consideration. It is therefore his intention to introduce new legislation during the current session of Parliament to modernize federal juvenile law, to remedy existing deficiencies, and to reflect prevailing attitudes and practices.
The new legislation, to be known as the Young Offenders Act, is the result of extensive study and consultation by the
Young Offenders Act
federal government. I must say it includes many provisions drafted by the previous administration under the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark). We, too, had a lot of input. The hon. member for Durham-Northumberland (Mr. Lawrence), who was then solicitor general, put this package together. Major associations and groups, private agencies and the general public were also consulted. This consultation process has had a major impact in formulating the underlying principles and the over-all substance of the proposed legislation. It is probably realistic to conclude that this consultation process has now yielded its maximum benefits. While it has become abundantly clear that unanimity on ail aspects of the new legislation was not realized, consensus has been achieved on the need for legislative reform and on the major thrust and provisions of the proposed new legislation. Furthermore, the reforms in the proposed new legislation are long overdue and necessary for Canadian society as a whole and for our young people in particular. It is neither desirable nor justifiable to continue to administer juvenile justice in Canada under the outdated legislative prescriptions of the current Juvenile Delinquents Act, a statute enacted in 1908. Delays which continue to deprive our youth and the public of law in keeping with the times and incorporating those universally accepted elements of reform must cease.
I forgot to mention that I am delighted today to follow such eloquent speakers as the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Malone) and the hon. member for Pembina (Mr. Elzinga), both of whom I admire very much. Their eloquent speeches today have added much to the input of this particular bill.
Hear, hear!

Young Offenders Act
Mr. Speaker, I knew I was addressing the Chair and I would now like to address all the constituents in Ottawa West on your behalf.
