Hear, hear!
What about Ottawa-Carleton?

In affording society protection from illegal behaviour, it is to be recognized that young persons require supervision, discipline and control, but also because of their state of dependence and level of development and maturity, young persons have special needs and require guidance and assistance. Where it is not inconsistent with the protection of society, consideration should be given to using alternative social and legal measures for dealing with young persons who have committed offences which come within the jurisdiction of this act.
In determining the responsibility of young persons under this act, it should be recognized that young persons have rights and freedoms, including those stated in the Canadian Bill of Rights; particularly the right to be heard and to participate in the processes that lead to decisions which affect them, as well as special guarantees of these rights.
In the application of this act, the rights and freedoms of young persons include the right to the least interference with freedom, having regard to the protection of society, the needs of young persons, and the interests of their families. Young persons have the right, in every instance where their rights or freedoms may be affected by this act, to be informed of what those rights and freedoms are.
It is recognized that parents have responsibility for the care and supervision of their children. Therefore, young persons should be removed from parental supervision, either partly or entirely, only when all other measures that provide for continuing parental supervision are inappropriate.
Let us look at some of the major substantive provisions of the proposed legislation. I am not a lawyer, but those of my colleagues who are in the legal profession who have assessed this bill very carefully, have told me what has happened. I am told that the provision dealing with offences is in keeping with the recommendation of the Law Reform Commission of Canada to exclude less serious conduct from the application of the criminal law, conduct that could better be dealt with through our social or legal means. Thus it would remain for the provinces to amend existing child welfare and youth protection legislation if necessary to deal with less serious status behaviour and to establish the process by which provincial and municipal offences would be dealt with in the future.
In addition, it would remove one of the more discriminatory and highly criticized features of the Juvenile Delinquents Act whereby certain types of behaviour by young persons are criminalized, although the same behaviour for an adult would not constitute an offence.
I shall now deal with the provision on the age of applicability, in other words the minimum age. Under the proposed new legislation, the age of criminal responsibility would be raised from 7 to 12 years. It was universally agreed that under the current Juvenile Delinquents Act the age of 7 was too young for criminal proceedings. Fourteen years of age was suggested by two provinces; the remaining provinces and the majority of other persons consulted favoured 12 years. Furthermore, statistics indicate that a significant number of youths aged 12 and 13 are in conflict with the law.
Let us look at the maximum age. While the federal government recognizes the desirability of standardizing a maximum age across the country, the consultations, while also favouring a uniform age, have failed to achieve agreement as to what that age should be. The Solicitor General recommends that the new legislation provide for a uniform maximum age under 16 years. This would appear to be in accord with the preferred view of the majority of provinces as well as that of most groups and persons consulted. Nevertheless, this should be left to the jurisdiction of the provinces.
The Solicitor General is prepared to consider the establishment of a uniform maximum age at a level under either 17 or 18 years in the event that agreement among the provinces can be achieved. It should be noted that under the Juvenile Delinquents Act, the maximum age is set at under 16 years with provision for the establishment of a level of 17 or 18 years in any given province. Currently the age level in the various provinces and territories is as follows: Under 18 years in Quebec and Manitoba; under 17 years in British Columbia and under 16 years in all remaining provinces and territories. In Newfoundland, where the Juvenile Delinquents Act does not apply, the age under provincial legislation is 17 years.
I consider the involvement of parents to be very important. The new act will recognize the primary responsibility of parents for the care and supervision of their children and the necessity for their involvement in the judicial process. Parents would be notified of proceedings, encouraged and, when necessary, ordered to attend. As well, parents would be allowed to make representations regarding the disposition and application for a transfer to adult court or a review of any disposition.
I now come to legal representation. In contrast to the Juvenile Delinquents Act which is silent on the rights of young persons, the new legislation would expressly articulate the rights afforded them. The right to retain and instruct counsel at any stage of proceedings, including instances when diversion measures are considered, would be recognized and protected by special provisions. For example, parents would be notified of any arrest or detention proceedings against the young person; all summons or warrants directed to a young person would contain a notification of a right to cancel, and youth court judges would be required to advise a young person appearing before the youth court of his rights.
Of course, in cases of conflict of interest, the young person would have counsel independent of his parents.

I wish to thank the hon. member for Saskatoon West (Mr. Hnatyshyn) for his legal consultation. We had some close collaboration so that I could put forward these remarks in the debate this afternoon.

He did not write my speech but, with his great legal mind, he did permit me some consultation without charging me a fee.

The provision on predisposition reports and assessments is only a paragraph or so long. The legislation will permit greater use of assessments and predisposition reports. In appropriate cases where one or more of the following conditions are present, namely physical or mental illness or disorder, learning disability or mental retardation, medical examinations and psychological or psychiatric assessments will be undertaken when ordered by the youth court.
Predisposition reports will be mandatory when an application for transfer to adult court is being considered and prior to the imposition of any custodial sentence.
With regard to screening and diversion, the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) gave a dissertation on that subject this afternoon. I will not go into that part of the bill in the short time available to me. Maybe my learned colleague will speak on that.
I would now like to deal with detention of young persons prior to a court disposition. The young offenders act would set out a precise procedure to be applied when detention of a young person is being considered. In this regard, it proposes that the rules and criteria regarding bail as set out in the Criminal Code should apply, with some modifications to meet the special circumstances of young persons. Legislation would also require that parents be notified, and it would provide that, as a general rule, young persons who are held in detention be kept separate and apart from adult offenders. The youth court would have jurisdiction to hear all bail applications concerning any offence involving a young person and would have the power to release the young person in the care of a responsible adult in lieu of detaining him in custody, where it appears that adequate control can be exercised and the attendance of the young person can be guaranteed. With regard to this phase of the legislation, 1 had close consultation with my colleague, the House leader from this side, the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker). I wish to thank him for that part of my dissertation this afternoon.
Let us next consider the transfer to adult courts. There will be exceptional cases where the proposed legislation for dealing with young persons must be overridden because the gravity of the case demands an exception to the philosophy and practices of the youth court. In such cases, new legislation would
Young Offenders Act
provide explicit guidelines and procedures for the transfer of cases to adult court. As such, the proposed transfer provisions would apply only to young persons age 14 and above, as is the case under the Juvenile Delinquents Act, and in addition, would set out detailed factors for consideration by the youth court judge in arriving at a decision whether or not to transfer the case to the adult court. Consideration of a predisposition report would be mandatory prior to making a transfer order.
Let us look at dispositions. The proposed legislation would make available to the youth court a wide and flexible range of sentencing dispositions geared to meet the needs of young persons, to protect society and to take into consideration in appropriate cases the rights of the victims of crime. The dispositions available are an absolute discharge, a fine to a maximum of $1,000, a restitution or compensation order for actual loss or damage to property, loss of income or special damages arising as a result of personal injury; order for compensation in kind or by way of personal service, community service order, probation to a maximum of two years, committal to intermittent or continuous custody not to exceed two years, provision for ancillary conditions, that is an order of forfeiture of illegally possessed goods, prohibition of firearms, etc.
It is worthy of special note that all dispositions would be of a determinate nature and that the youth court would retain exclusive jurisdiction over the case of a young person. It would not be possible to transfer jurisdiction of the case to provincial law and authorities, as is now the practice in some cases under section 21 of the Juvenile Delinquents Act. In such cases, a young person does not remain subject to the jurisdiction of the juvenile court but is further dealt with solely pursuant to provincial law. As criminal legislation, the proposed act acknowledges that this practice should be discontinued, as the judiciary is seen as that body which should decide the extent to which custodial and other measures depriving a young person of his liberty and freedom should be utilized to ensure the safety of communities and its citizens. Once a judicial sentence is pronounced, it is inconsistent that such decisions be unilaterally altered by provincial social service or correctional authorities: Furthermore, a young person should have ongoing access to the court for purposes of review.
On the other hand, in order to afford provinces sufficient flexibility to plan and implement effective programming for young persons serving custodial sentences, the provincial director would, following committal to custody by the court, have the authority to determine the level and place of custody in which the young person should be held. Custody would be broadly defined to mean containment or restraint in a variety of places or facilities ranging from group homes, community training residences, wilderness camps and child care or correctional institutions. The meaning of custody is intended to be flexible so as to allow movement within programs and facilities, as well as temporary releases to the community, without judicial approval. In addition, the new legislation would provide a procedure for the release of a young person from

Thank you, Mr. Speaker.
There is provision in this bill for appeals, the privacy of youth court proceedings, fingerprinting and photographing. I think my colleagues might want to deal with those matters, but one thing which is of real importance to me, to many parents and many social workers, is the appointment of judges. It has been suggested that Canada adopt the European system of appointing juvenile court judges. In Europe judges are trained as career judges. They are not appointed from the bar, as is the case in Canada. Previous practice of law, is, of course, an indispensable asset to a juvenile court judge. However, in addition to this experience, all juvenile court judges should have an extensive knowledge of social sciences. Not only should they have extensive knowledge of social sciences but they should also be former parents. They should have had children. They should know what the responsibilities are.
Special training programs should be developed. In addition, periodic consultation sessions involving judges, provincial authorities, lawyers, police and behavioural scientists would allow for valuable information flow and provide access to new trends and developments in law and social sciences.
The Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) is a very learned man and a director of one of the fine universities here. He should pass this suggestion on to some of his colleagues. People other than just people in law should become judges. Particularly for juvenile court judges there has to be a human dimension.
May 29, 1981

Not everything is just found in the book. Not everything is writs and torts. Something has to come from the heart. One has to see and assess. Members of Parliament live with their constituents. They listen to confessions weekend upon weekend. They know what all the problems are about. Perhaps former members of Parliament should have first right of refusal. It seems strange that the report of the Solicitor General's committee on proposals for new legislation is silent in this regard. Surely the duties and responsibilities of the youth court are as vital and as far-reaching as those of any court in Canada.
In conclusion-and in retrospect-the Juvenile Delinquents Act in action has established a reasonable track record, as its length of tenure will testify. Most of the potential abuses and incursions upon the basic rights of young people when they have occurred-and when they have been appealed-have been quickly corrected in the higher courts.
The bulk of the recommendations which are going to the committee are addressed to technical and procedural matters, and I hope when this bill goes to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs, a close look will be given to the bill and many of the new recommendations will be included.
Even if limitless resources were available, perhaps the present system would remain inadequate because it is unable to treat the whole problem. The whole problem concerns problems of education, recreation, religion, health and parental supervision. These problems cannot be solved by due process. We need fully organized community resources which can view and understand the needs of a child as part of a larger whole, the family and its community. The family situation of the juvenile alone is worthy of another half hour. If the family does not stay together, all these problems are bound to occur, but I do not think I will go into that this afternoon.
Third reading.

At the present time we have dozens of different governments involved as well as countless numbers of private individuals and agencies. There is a lack of communication and, in many instances, fragmentation and mistrust.

In this day and age that situation changes from month to month. There is a new morality, and we must look at the matter in that light.
I will conclude by saying that I appreciate this opportunity to speak on this matter. I hope to speak a little more about the family unit perhaps at third reading.

It is certainly a bill of some importance to all members in the House, and perhaps most specifically, as the parliamentary secretary opposite would know, to those of us who represent urban ridings because there is, for anyone who follows what is happening in a centre such as metropolitan Toronto, a serious concern about the rise of crime among adolescents and particularly the rise in violent crime among young people. One of my colleagues earlier in the debate made an intervention at some length on this question, and there are a number of quite scary statistics which the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona's (Mr. Kilgour) listed in his remarks which are well worth reading and actually were drawn from one of the speeches made in the Senate. I would like to say just a few words about the amendment before the House, but before I do so perhaps I could indicate

May 29, 1981
Young Offenders Act
my strong view that the need for this bill is overdue. Many of its provisions, which finally recognize children and young adults as persons, are extremely welcome in this day and age. I speak specifically of the provisions with regard to bail and the right to counsel, most specifically those that would formalize and regularize to some degree the ability of a court to apply the tactics that lawyers-not being one I use the phrase advisedly-describe as diversions. Frankly, we have had some experience in our juvenile courts in this country, some in Toronto specifically, with attempts to show young people that the right response to a wrongful act-and it is at least to some degree their responsibility to understand that they have committed a wrongful act-is to avoid as far as possible putting those people in official institutions. The reason is that there is very clear evidence that if we can avoid putting people in institutions, we have a much greater chance of avoiding a longterm problem. 1 am thinking specifically of some remarks made earlier in the debate by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Cooper) when he referred to some very important evidence in an essay entitled "Middle Class Delinquency" by a Mr. Leblanc and also evidence from a Mr. Letkemen laying out very clearly the effect of a policy that leads to a substantial number of young people finding their way into reformatories as a method of trying to solve the problem. The evidence is clear that if we continue this policy we will create in the future an ever larger group of criminals.
It is for that reason specifically that I welcome the formalization of the provisions of diversion that would allow the courts to find alternative methods of giving young people an understanding that they have done something wrong and must pay for it, without having to put them into jails or reformatories. I think that is vital.
1 should, however, like to put one other matter on the record which was referred to earlier. It is with regard to a provision in the act concerning bail and evidence rights, a provision about which 1 am somewhat worried and which I hope will be raised in committee. It is referred to elsewhere in Hansard but 1 want to make sure it is known that I feel this way about clause 56(3) which states:
The requirements set out in paragraphs (2)(b), (c) and (d) do not apply in respect of oral statements where they are volunteered by the young people to a peace officer or other persons in authority before that person has had a reasonable opportunity to comply with those requirements.
I have a feeling, Mr. Speaker, that this provision leads potentially to some very difficult circumstances, and 1 hope it is checked thoroughly in committee because I find it hard to believe that we would expect somebody who is 12, 13 or 14 to have any sense of his rights under the law prior to speaking to his lawyer. I hope that that clause will be either removed or modified in such a way that that potential loophole for the misuse of evidence is closed.
Perhaps the most important matter before us today, as I indicated when I started my remarks, is the amendment put by the hon. member for Durham-Northumberland (Mr. Lawrence) dealing with what he described, and we as a party believe to be, as the major problem in the bill. We have stressed this over and over again, and I know other hon.
members are aware of how we feel about this, but I think it is absolutely vital that it be made clear that it is very difficult for us to accept the idea that the age at which one is no longer a young person before the law shall be different from province to province.
There is no great magic as to why we are opposed ot it. The reason is very simple and it was stated most clearly by members in this House who described the different circumstances of someone who stood on one side of the bridge from Ottawa to Hull and committed an offence, and someone of the same age on the other side who committed an offence. One might be an offender under the law while the other might not be if the provinces adopted different laws or had opted out differently. Clearly that is wrong. Surprisingly it is not wrong in the eyes of a government which has maintained throughout the constitutional debate that it is precisely those opting out provisions on rights that are, at least in their view, the reason for moving so quickly and unilaterally on a charter of rights.
If you believed, Mr. Speaker, that the need to enshrine rights across this country is so important that we should adopt the unilateral process which this government has adopted, a process which is divisive in a country used to operating as a partnership, you would think the government should take the position that it wants to bring in this bill with provincial consent provisions relating to a fixed common age. My personal view, for the reasons I expressed earlier, about keeping people out of the formal institutions, is that the age should be 18 not 16. I am cognizant of the fact that the problem has been to get provincial consent and it may be that, for other reasons, there will be consent to the age of 16. I only wish that the government had obtained that consent before drafting the bill because what we will be forced to deal with, if this bill is not changed, is a different application of the law with respect to the same crime, if that is not too harsh a word for what we are talking about, and that seems to me to be a shame.
Let me therefore conclude my remarks, Mr. Speaker. I did not intend to speak very long today and will not do so because there are others who wish to speak as well, but certainly in a centre like metropolitan Toronto this change in our legislation will be extremely welcome. I will support anything that makes our young people bear the responsibility for their actions and at the same time keeps them out of the formal institutions which produce more criminal behaviour, because it can only be in our long-term interest to try to make our young people understand they must not break the law, but at the same time to make sure we do not turn them into criminals.

The government would be well advised to make inroads with respect to consistency rather than using its bulldozer approach to every issue of federal-provincial concern in the country by saying, "Henceforth we will have uniformity across the country. Regardless of whether you are from Gaspe or Saskatoon West, you will march to the same drummer. There will be no concern with respect to regional differences and aspirations." That is the attitude of the government. It is a blockbuster, blockhead approach to politics in Canada.
My colleagues have said that we think the federal government should assert itself on this issue. There is an important distinction in the attitude of the two parties. In fact, a significant minority in the NDP has taken the same position with respect to the whole constitutional issue.
I want to ensure that this bill goes to committee. We now know what are the circumstances. The committee is occupied with the freedom of information legislation about the improvement of which hon. members of my party, under the leadership of the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker), are making constructive suggestions. The committee will be concerned with that piece of legislation for a week or two. I want to put the government on notice that it is our considered opinion that immediately after this stage of our deliberations we should have an opportunity to hear representations in committee from people affected by this legislation. We cannot summon the representatives of the provinces before the committee; it would be improper to do so. We should give notice- and perhaps by this speech I will be giving notice-to provincial authorities that we welcome their input with respect to the improvement of the operation of the bill. We should listen to these people, if they are prepared to come and give evidence before the committee. We should take an intensive look at the bill. We in this party are very anxious to make progress. The matter has languished on the desks of Liberal solicitors general for over ten years.
For the short time we were in government, at least we took the initiative. The hon. member for Durham-Northumberland took legislative action and put the proposal before Parliament at the earliest possible date.
With those very few words, I remind the House about our dissatisfaction with the manner in which the government handled this particular piece of legislation-its silence, indifference and insensitivity.
Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL FOR A NATIONAL NUTRITION PROGRAM
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of supporting in principle the implementation of a national nutrition program to be funded jointly by the federal and provincial governments, which program would
1.	improve the health of young Canadians;
2.	help educate children and parents as to the value of proper nutrition; and
3.	help eliminate any surplus of nutritive foods produced by Canadian farmers.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the motion which I have proposed today is one which I can take no personal pride in conceiving. It is an idea which has been proposed by some of the most knowledgeable and responsible people in this country. In March of 1973 the National Council of Welfare published a document entitled "one child, one chance". In their report they proposed the following:
That a nation-wide system of school meals be established for all our children, as a preventive health service, on a federal-provincial cost-sharing basis. Where funds do not permit the establishment of universal programs from the outset, first priority within such a system should be given to the initiation of school breakfast programs in disadvantaged areas and in areas where children must
travel long distances to reach school. Where such programs can be initiated only in stages, we wish to see nutritious meals provided first to the youngest children.
The report by the National Council of Welfare was followed up by a report prepared by the federal-provincial nutrition committee of the Department of National Health and Welfare entitled "Guidelines for School Food Programs in Canada". This report was published in June of 1976. In outlining the rationale for improved school programs they said in part:
The need for school food programs has always been of concern to parents, educators and health workers and has recently become an important issue in all parts of the country. This has been pinpointed in the recommended priorities of the Nutrition Canada reports-
The report went on to say:
The consequences of poor nutrition have a significant effect on the ability of students to benefit from their school education.
School nutrition programs are not unheard of in Canada. In the city of Winnipeg there have been such programs since 1975. The program began in Winnipeg after a good deal of controversy with a $290,000 budget. Some 650 school children were provided with lunches at school. At that time the program was attacked, but today, because of demonstrated need, the program has a budget of $407,000, 50 per cent of which is provided by the provincial government. About 1,700 children are receiving breakfast in 25 schools at a cost of $127,000, while 6,000 receive nutrition education. Despite this, it has become common knowledge, as reported in the daily Winnipeg newspapers, that so great are the needs that many children are appearing at agencies such as the Salvation Army, and other core area institutions, to obtain food on weekends and holidays. The city and the province are so concerned about what will happen this summer when the schools are not functioning that they have established a special committee to look into the problem.
The schools of Montreal have had a nutrition program for a number of years. I have in my hand a document dated "Spring, 1976" entitled "Nutrition/Education". The first paragraph of the document reads:
The School Council of the Island of Montreal has officially adopted a subsidized food policy: its aim is to make students familiar with the basic principles of good nutrition.
The document goes on:
Why a food policy?
It is a well known fact that a person's state of health influences his behaviour and energy, and that good eating habits can promote better health.
In outlining what they do, the Council said:
-school cafeteria menus must conform to the document... Nutrition in Schools, published by the Quebec Department of Social Affairs;
I find the following remark very interesting:
-school cafeteria menus will no longer include:
-deep-fried foods such as french fries, do-nuts... , sugary foods that cause
tooth decay such as candy, soft drinks, chewing gum, potato chips-
Not only is the Council providing feeding programs but it is trying to educate the students as to what kinds of foods they should eat. They encourage the students to stay away from junk foods which are so often eaten in today's hurried society.
May 29, 1981

Since 1976 in the city of Toronto, the Toronto Board of Education has had policies assisting school and community organizations in the implementation of lunch and school-aged day care, which are referred to in their policy as "comprehensive care programs". Currently, 59 schools offer lunch programs and 22 schools offer school-aged day care. In a survey of 106 elementary schools conducted on December I, 1975, by the curriculum program division of the Toronto Board of Education it was reported that 76 elementary schools were taking advantage of lunchroom supervision assistance. The board, in its report, outlined the kind of nutrition programs they have. They have a variety of programs, Type A to Type E, as follows: type A provides a bag lunch; type B consists of soup, milk, apple, plus a bag lunch; type C consists of soup, milk, apple, plus a bag lunch; type D consists of a hot meal catered or cooked at the school; and, type E is also a hot meal either catered or cooked at the school.
The reason that the cities of Winnipeg, Toronto and Montreal have such programs, and I am sure I could add a number of other cities to the list, is that they know how much these kinds of programs are required. I have already indicated that in my own city of Winnipeg, despite the fact that we have had school nutrition programs in 20 or more of the core area schools, it is now becoming apparent that there are still elementary school children who are not receiving the kind of nutrition they need. Indeed, in a full-page article which appeared just a couple of weeks ago in the Winnipeg Free Press, the principal of one school reported:
George Heshka, chairman of the Winnipeg school board's nutrition extension committee, took an inner-city student to lunch one Monday many months ago and still recalls what he learned.
He saw the hamburger fast disappearing and asked the youngster what he had eaten the day before.
"Mr. Heshka, I didn't eat anything," came the reply.
"Why not?" Heshka asked.
"Because yesterday was a holiday and you don't eat on holidays."
I could go on, Mr. Speaker, but the facts are clear that in my city-and I am sure the facts are not different in many other cities-agencies such as the Salvation Army and the Rossbrook centre, and many others, are finding youngsters who are simply not receiving at home the kind of food they need, which is affecting their attendance at school.
It is affecting the kind of attention they can give to their classes. It is having a disastrous effect on their physical and mental health and on their ability to absorb the kind of education which they ought to be able to receive.
There is one other reason as to why I believe such a program would be useful, not only to the children who attend our schools from one end of Canada to the other, but also to Canadian farmers, and would improve their lot in a substantial way. We have or have had substantial surpluses of most of the major food products produced on Canadian farms. Let me just list some of the food items which, in recent years, have been in surplus amounts. There have been surpluses of butter and skim milk powder. I am told that last year 130 million pounds of
Nutrition
skim milk powder were sold to countries outside of Canada at a substantial loss in order to remove the surplus. We had substantial surpluses of evaporated milk which we again sold to foreign countries at a loss. We are now running a surplus of 750 million dozen eggs a week. We are losing about 40 cents a dozen when we sell them on the world market. We have or have had surpluses of apples, potatoes, onions, carrots, pears and peaches. I am sure that the list which I just read is not a complete list of the surpluses we have or have had of farm products in recent years. Many of these products have been purchased, processed and stored by the Agricultural Products Board, which is a division of Agriculture Canada, and have been sold at a loss.
So, what I am suggesting is that if this kind of program were funded jointly by the federal-provincial governments, not only would it help to improve the nutritional standards and the health of our young people in this country who are attending our schools, but it would also help, in a marked, substantial way, to stabilize the purchase and the use of the surplus food products which are being produced in this country by Canadian farmers. I could compare this in a small way with the success which the United States has had in disposing of a substantial part of its surplus agricultural products through its food stamp plan. Through this program, millions of American citizens in the lower income groups have been able to supplement and improve their diet through the purchase of surplus food produced in the United States at special reduced prices.
So without any further words on my part, I want to urge hon. members of the House to support this resolution which 1 think would benefit, as I have said, the young people in this country. At the same time, in a very practical way, it would benefit the farmers in this country who have been able to produce food in such substantial quantities that we have surpluses of many of our food products.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Celine Hervieux-Payette (Parliamentary Secretary to Solicitor General):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
subsubtopic: PROPOSAL FOR A NATIONAL NUTRITION PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it gives me great pleasure to discuss with my colleague, the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) the subject of his motion, which, in my opinion, is essential to the future of Canadians, namely improving the health of young Canadians. I believe that no government member could object to such a motion. I would like to tell my colleagues about my experience within various organizations concerned with nutrition.
First, Mr. Speaker, as legislative secretary to the Quebec Minister of Social Affairs, I worked in close co-operation with departmental officials to develop a provincial nutrition program, and I should mention that I believe provincial authorities are primarily responsible for implementing a program in this area. At the time, we had identified target populations, because, when we deal with matters such as preventive programs or health improvement, as you are aware, Mr. Speaker, we are dealing with major issues and programs which aim at

May 29, 1981
Nutrition
changing the mentality of people, and they require a lot of time and money.
One of the target groups, Mr. Speaker, were future mothers. Under a prenatal program, these women received specific instruction concerning their own nutrition and that of their baby. Indeed, Mr. Speaker, I believe that it is in specific situations that a government can implement special programs designed to improve the health of Canadians. In that case, future generations of Canadians will benefit along with their mothers. 1 believe that at the time we were teaching the basic principles of good nutrition, which were certainly beneficial since statistics show a decrease in the number of infant deaths due to increasingly well-balanced diet. I shall not go into the details of these policies, Mr. Speaker, 1 believe that they are well administered provincially, but I think the Canadian government has urged the provinces to take specific action, by developing a comprehensive preventive policy.
I would like to refer to the policy statement made by the Hon. Marc Lalonde when he was minister of National Health and Welfare since, after all, he developed the elements of a policy which are still applied today throughout Canada, and I am proud to say, Mr. Speaker, even throughout the world. Indeed, the former Minister of National Health and Welfare also acted as consultant for the World Health Organization and described on the international level the Canadian experience and made statements of policy on behalf of Canada in this regard. We can therefore be proud not only that we have a policy in this field, but also that we have helped to improve health standards throughout the world.
Another group, Mr. Speaker, which benefits from a preventive or special education program is that of schoolchildren throughout Canada. This group is more easily reached. It benefits from special programs, and it is my opinion, Mr. Speaker, that an examination will show that each province has acted in the best interest of schoolchildren with regard to nutrition. 1 would like to refer in this regard to our experience in Quebec, since I can say that we have made significant progress in that area. And such progress is effectively related not only to the first object of the motion introduced by the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) but also to the third point of his motion which is: "To help to eliminate any surplus of nutritive foods produced by Canadian farmers." Indeed, Mr. Speaker, I am pleased at last to note that after a few years, the Quebec government, in co-operation with school boards, has made it possible for young children in primary grades to get free milk at school.
We know that Quebec is an important dairy producer and I think that such policy is liable not only to promote agriculture and be an incentive to dairy producers but will obviously be used to teach basic nutrition to our schoolchildren. In that respect, as a former president of a regional school board, the regional school board of Le Gardeur, I can say that the
implementation of that policy has worked smoothly for the benefit of every segment of our community. The youngsters who had not been informed by their parents about the importance of milk as a nutrient, were told about it at school and they will probably never forget those facts.
Of course, the addition of milk at school in the child's diet is but one thing. Each year, most Quebec school boards have a nutrition week during which all the basic teaching aids and all the tools of the school board are made available to the public in order to help young students become aware of the value of good nutrition. As far as we are concerned, one of the most successful experiments was a fruit and vegetable tasting at school, prepared in co-operation with the parents, the school committees and even the school cafeteria, which agreed to forgo the profits from one meal to give the students the opportunity to taste a variety of mostly Canadian vegetables and fruits which, for many students, often was a new taste experience.
We must not delude ourselves, Mr. Speaker, it is first and foremost in the home that the principles of good nutrition are learned, and in that respect I think we are fortunate in Canada to have such quality products available. We do not have to go that far back to realize how much the quality, the quantity and the variety of foodstuff have improved. In that respect, Mr. Speaker, I can recall my experience at Steinberg, where I was in charge of consumer relations. I can certainly say that the consumption of fruit and vegetables has increased markedly whereas there has been a decrease in the purchase of less nutritional foods. There has indeed been a per capita decrease in the quantity of meat consumed which has been compensated by an increase in the consumption of fruit and vegetables.
Mr. Speaker, I think that is the result of well integrated policies designed to educate the public and our young people in particular. These policies have indeed led to a change in eating habits. And I am certainly happy to see that the action of the federal government, supported by the provinces, has produced such positive results. In that regard, Mr. Speaker, it should be noted at this stage that the department of National Health and Welfare has made available to Canadian families a guide entitled The Canadian Food Guide or the Nutrition Guide, which is available from the members' offices in their ridings or through the department's information offices.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I think it would be a good idea to urge all our fellow Canadians who have not yet obtained this food guide to get one. It is simple and easy to read. It provides a complete list of nutritive foods. Because I have a family, I intend, among other things, to find a place for this guide somewhere in the kitchen or stick it on the refrigerator door, so that everybody in the home may be reminded of the basic nutrients necessary for a good and healthy nutrition, and help those who might be tempted to indulge or, even worse, to overindulge, and also to make them understand that a healthy and well-balanced diet includes various types of foods which
May 29, 1981

are equally good, but which should complement one another. 1 do not want to go over each and every one of these nutrients, but simply urge all Canadian consumers to get this guide which, everything considered, shows the way to wholesome and well-balanced nutrition.
On the other hand, Mr. Speaker, I suggest it is important to show that when work in that field was carried out within the Department of National Health and Welfare there was consultation indeed. Of course, however significant the role of the Canadian government in that sector, it must be admitted that the means to reach the people are in provincial rather than federal hands. That is why I think the initiatives are excellent, but in the end they cannot be anything more than initiatives which may be encouraging and I do not believe that a massive campaign would totally change eating habits. People will agree with me, Mr. Speaker, that a simple reduction in the consumption of fat or sugar is not an easy goal to reach, nor something which can be accomplished overnight. It is always easier to make young children develop such habits than to try to change them in adulthood.
On the other hand, I think that most documents published by the federal department reveal that in this field there has to be adaptation. Sedentary working habits call for an eating pattern which differs from that of a worker in the field, in northern regions, in huge petroleum projects or again in construction. Those people who work 12 hours a day cannot follow the same standards and their eating requirements are different. Therefore certain basic principles have to be respected and I think that each person must still adapt the fundamental rules of nutrition to his activities and his age.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to point out that whatever initiative we may take in future it would be contrary to a liberal philosophy to resort to coercion in that field. Just as all people who are concerned by this question, including the hon. member for Winnipeg North, I think that the new trend toward eating frozen foods or fried foods-fast foods, as they are called-is indeed the latest fashion. Such foods are in great demand nowadays; perhaps they do require a little less preparation time, but still it is appropriate to sound a warning against an abusive consumption of those meals. I do not intend to belittle that type of food, but instead I would urge Canadians to show moderation in their intake of those foods because they do have a rather high fat content and such a steady diet might eventually lead to health problems.
So, Mr. Speaker, I agree that a nutrition policy is needed and must be implemented. Such a policy has already been enunciated by the Canadian government and various ways of carrying it out are being considered. On the other hand, Mr. Speaker, I feel it is important to take note of what is already being done and that is really what the pragmatic observations I have just made were intended to underline.
Nutrition
Today there is a set of nutrition recommendations which has been accepted as a base for programs by federal and provincial authorities. I should like to state these in point form, if you will permit me, Mr. Speaker.
The first recommendation would be the consumption of a nutritionally adequate diet as outlined in the Canada food guide. This is the first recommendation that we are following. The second is a reduction in calories of fat to 35 per cent of total calories. This includes a source of polyunsaturated fatty acid in the diet. The third recommendation is the consumption of a diet which emphasizes whole grain products, fruits and vegetables, and minimizes alcohol, salt and refined sugars. The fourth recommendation is the prevention and control of obesity through reducing excess consumption of calories and increasing physical activity. Precautions should be taken so that no deficiency of vitamins and minerals occur when total calories are reduced.
These recommendations as stated were accepted in a 1978 cabinet discussion paper called "Integration of Nutrition into Food Strategy". They are being implemented across Canada as a result of a series of consultations. A major consultation was with the provincial departments of health through the work of the federal-provincial subcommittee on nutrition. Once this consultation was completed over 50 national associations were asked to discuss, endorse and support the implementation of the recommendations. These include health groups such as the Canadian Medical Association, the Canadian Nursing Association, as well as the food industry, retailers and processors, and groups such as the Agricultural Institute of Canada.
The nutrition recommendations are becoming an integral part of nutrition programs across Canada. Implementing them into programs has highlighted the need to improve existing education programs. There has been confusion between the recommendations which represent our position and other goals, guidelines, and those from other organizations and countries. Many articles were prepared for journals in this country and others for Britain and the U.S.A.
In order to improve nutritional health, we have to learn more about Canadians' knowledge and understanding of nutrition. In this regard we are collecting information about what Canadians think and know about nutrition. For example, in 1979, the Department of National Health and Welfare undertook a study on nutrition. Over 1,600 Canadians across the country were interviewed. Most of them felt that a sensible diet was important to them. They defined a sensible diet as eating a variety of foods, eating at regular times and not eating foods that are too sweet or greasy. A sensible diet was important to them because they said it meant fewer health problems and generally better health. However, the people surveyed did not believe that all Canadians generally followed a sensible diet.

May 29, 1981
Nutrition
It has been said many times that it is difficult for people to change eating habits. Yet in this study, four out of ten people had made a major change in their eating habits over the past year. The change was positive. They cut back on certain foods and increased their intake of other more nutritious foods.
From these recommendations, it is apparent that federal and provincial authorities are working together for a better program and for the implementation of guidelines which will result in better health for Canadians.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to follow the hon. member for Montreal-Mercier (Mrs. Hervieux-Payette) who indicated that the federal and provincial governments are now working together with respect to nutrition. I recall her words at the beginning of her statement when she said that no member of the government would oppose such an idea, that is the idea in the motion.
The motion is very clear. It states:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of supporting in principle the implementation of a national nutrition program to be funded jointly by the federal and provincial governments, which program would
1.	improve the health of young Canadians;
2.	help educate children and parents as to the value of proper nutrition; and
3.	help eliminate any surplus of nutritive foods produced by Canadian farmers.
I want to congratulate the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow). It appears from what the hon. member from Montreal-Mercier has said, we will experience one of those rare moments in the House when the government permits a motion to pass, because she stated that no member of the government would oppose such an idea, meaning the government will not use the usual method of talking out a motion. Therefore, I do not expect to hear a speech from any member in the House today that will carry this matter beyond five o'clock.
I suspect the compassionate member for Guelph (Mr. Schroder) would not make a speech to impede the hon. member for London-Middlesex (Mr. Bloomfield), if he intends to say a few words; I trust that the hon. member for Sarnia-Lambton (Mr. Cullen), the hon. member for Hull (Mr. Isabelle), the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia), the hon. member for Chateauguay (Mr. Watson) or even the Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Privy Council (Mr. Collenette), will not make speeches today carrying this matter beyond five o'clock because members on the government side who have spoken thus far have said they are not opposed to the motion.

I will talk for only two more minutes because I want to see the motion go through.
There is a second thing which should be encouraging for the hon. member for Winnipeg North. A few days ago in question period, the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) accused my party of adopting a position similar to that of the President of
the United States, namely that we would want to see the elimination of food programs. That is not so. But I want to say that if this motion is not passed today, it would be open for each one of us to say that members of the Liberal party are not prepared to see a similar program in Canada.

I think it is incumbent on the House when something goes to the root of a matter that can be quite important to certain areas of the community not to support it just by rhetoric but to do so by action. This can be done in private members' hour by allowing the question to be reached on Friday afternoon before five o'clock.
I caution all of my dear friends on the other side of the House not to allow the support of the government, underlined by the hon. member for Montreal-Mercier when she said that no one would oppose such an idea, to be eroded and the motion to be talked out. I am certain this matter is of interest to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan). We all know that the Minister of Agriculture is at odds with his colleague, the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen), because of his support of the little person involved in agriculture who is having difficulty with interest rates and inflation. I think there are great problems on the other side-

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL FOR A NATIONAL NUTRITION PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to speak on this bill today. I would like to mention to the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker) that I am sure, being a fair-minded individual, he would not like to see us limited in our debate on this very important issue. Therefore, as long as there are members who have something to say, I am afraid we will be destined to speak.
We have heard quite a bit from the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) this afternoon and the hon. member from Montreal-Mercier (Mrs. Hervieux-Payette), so I will not repeat the information they have given.
May 29, 1981

I would like to talk about some attitudinal concepts which bring out the negative forces working against us in our attempt in the educational process to convince the people about what they are doing to their nutrition.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North is to be commended for bringing to our attention the need for continued emphasis on good nutrition and its importance to good health. It is a paradox that in Canada where we have access to an unlimited choice of wholesome food of unparalleled variety we continue to see malnutrition and poor nutrition. It continues to be apparent that having the facts is not always conducive to behavioural change. This is evident in many of the problem areas in our country today, but nowhere is it more evident than in the matter of our health, our eating habits in particular.
As an educator, I have long been aware of the infinite capacity of the human mind to resist the introduction of knowledge, but we must keep trying. We must never despair. If we could just match the promotional power of junk foods which pervades our every waking hour, if we could convince parents to make sure their children get a good start in life, and if we could convince adults to eat properly, not only would they help themselves but they would set a good example for the younger generation to follow. All of these would be good objectives, well within the possibility of attainment by our society.
I referred earlier to the promotion of foods which contribute to our state of poor nutrition. It is obvious that humans have never paid the same attention to nourishment for themselves as they have to nourishment of their animals. Many pets receive a better diet than do humans, each can or bag of feed showing a formulation which should ensure that the pet will be slim, healthy, active and with a shiny coat for life. The Canadian Veterinary Association, of which I have the honour to be a member, grants its seal of approval to pet foods which provide those foods and which attain the standards required. Recently, I observed a current television commercial promoting dog food. It stated, "Not a speck of cereal is present". Not long thereafter I saw another commercial promoting breakfast cereal, urging that it be fed to your children for that "get up and go energy". How can cereal be bad for your pet but good for your children?
It is tragedy that 800 million people live in a state of misery and desolation in the Third World. Many of them are removed from their misery by starving to death, not because they want to, but because they have no choice. How can we impress on our people that they have so many choices of pure, fresh, wholesome foods and that so often they make the wrong choices?
I take pride in my alma mater, the University of Guelph, which, through the faculty and staff of the college of family and consumer studies and department of nutrition, are dedicated to the science of nutrition and have made great contributions to the understanding of nutrition and the teaching of future teachers and scientists in that field.
Nutrition
It has been said, "It's too bad that youth has to be wasted on the young", but that is the way it is. There is no doubt that the greatest value in the educational program in nutrition will come from its application to this group. Many excellent school programs are now being given and the results are very positive.
I am pleased to discuss this motion regarding a national nutrition program and, in particular, a program which helps to educate children and parents as to the value of proper nutrition.
There is no doubt that the nutritional health of Canadians, particularly of children, is important to this government. We all know that during the time when a child is growing and developing from infancy to adolescence, he or she has special nutritional needs. There is a need to develop sensible eating habits which will last a lifetime. I would like to talk about some of the activities under way.
Education of children and parents about proper nutrition is a responsibility shared by many. One initiative undertaken by the federal government was a co-operative effort with the Canadian Pediatric Society to develop a position paper on breastfeeding. The paper was well received and was released in 1978 as a joint paper with the American Academy of Pediatrics. The timing was especially important because of the International Year of the Child in 1979. The Department of National Health and Welfare was represented on a national task force to promote breastfeeding established under the Canadian Pediatric Society during the International Year of the Child. The task force also included representatives from the LaLeche League, and the Society of Obstetricians and Gynecologists.
A program on nutrition was established at the educational level in order to increase the professionals' awareness of good nutrition. The government assumed a leadership role in producing and distributing an information kit called "Breastfeeding-An Awareness Program", to doctors, hospitals and public health nurses across the country. Over 55,000 copies of the kit have been distributed. The kit was enthusiastically endorsed by the federal-provincial advisory committee on community health services. It has also been endorsed by the Canadian Nurses Association, and acclaimed by international bodies such as the World Health Organization and UNICEF.
A publication entitled "Learning About Breastfeeding-A Selected Bibliography and Resource Guide" was prepared and circulated to professionals for their information. This kind of program represents a foundation for national nutrition programs because it helps us work toward a common goal. In this case, the common goal is to increase the number of mothers who breastfeed. This is a healthy way to give an infant a good start in life.
I could go on and talk about nutrition. However, I will end my discussion now so that other members who have a message to bring on this very important subject may have the opportunity to continue the debate.

Nutrition

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL FOR A NATIONAL NUTRITION PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the mover of the motion quite rightly took his 15 minutes to speak, and the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker), with his oratorical skills and enthusiasm, spoke a good 10 minutes on this motion. It is quite fair to claim that those of us on this side who are interested in this subject should also take some minutes in order to give their view of this motion.
It seems to me that the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) has brought a very fine idea to this House. Some components of his motion are being implemented in this country already. Some probably are not, but the whole thrust of his idea is more than sound, and I certainly compliment him for having taken this initiative. It is indeed a very fine one.
As just a side consideration, may I point out that in promoting the thoughts which are included in this motion, it might be helpful if each one of us in this House were to devote one newsletter to this topic when we write to our constituents. In that way we would be covering the country from coast to coast and giving impetus to some of the ideas which are inherent in the concept of a national nutrition program and in improving the quality of nutrition in Canada.
It is very timely to put forward a motion like this because we do live in a time, as a previous speaker has said, of fast food. Fast food is inexpensive, practical, can be acquired easily and certainly saves time, as the name implies.
At the same time, however, it contains additives, chemical colours and other products, the long-run effects of which we do not know. Therefore it is good for this House to stop for a moment and ponder about the trend of relying more and more on fast foods and giving up some of the good old-fashioned habits of previous times because what the second part of the hon. member's motion really implies is that we should have more faith and reliance on good old-fashioned homemade soup, homemade pasta and homemade pie and that we should rely more on milk, fresh fruit and vegetables and less on the fried food and the like which is easily available in the marketplace.
The motion moved by the hon. member for Winnipeg North raises a number of questions, and one of them has to do with how we can describe at the present time the health of our young people. On reviewing the information available, we find a publication produced by the Department of National Health and Welfare called "Nutrition Canada" which I suppose is available to everyone who wishes to purchase it at appropriate bookstores. It contains a study which brings out some interesting facts.
The study did not show instances of a real lack of nutrients in our eating patterns, but we do find some indicators of the fact that there is a need for improvement in a number of basic elements. For instance, the study shows that in the case of teenage girls, there is a need for improvement in their intake of iron. On a closer examination of food intake and nutrients consumed, we Find that there is a need for an increase on the part of the general public in the intake of vitamin A, vitamin D, vitamin C and calcium.
Many of the nutrition and health problems today are considered to be also the result of our lifestyle. From that study we learn that cardiovascular diseases, obesity, some forms of diabetes and dental caries are examples of problems which have links to poor eating habits. It is as plain as that. These are the kinds of health problems we want to avoid. Somehow the motion of the hon. member for Winnipeg North addresses itself to these matters in a straightforward and positive style.
A set of nutrition recommendations for Canadians has been accepted across Canada, and they are applicable to all Canadians over the age of two.
These recommendations were designed to provide a balance between nutrient deficiencies and excesses because we also have to watch the other side of the matter. The recommendations could be summarized in the following way: we should consume a nutritionally adequate diet as outlined in the book which was mentioned by a previous speaker entitled "Canada's Food Guide". Second, we should avoid the risk of becoming overweight through appropriate food selection and increased physical activity. Third, we should limit the total amount of fat, sugar, salt and alcohol in our diets. In the case of sugar and salt there have been some frightening adjectives used by some dieticians. I do not know whether we can accept them at face value, but certainly we are being warned about excessive use of both. I found them described in a book as being the white death. I do not know why we have come to use such exaggerated descriptions. Finally, we should increase our intake of vegetables, fruits and whole grain cereals and include sources of polyunsaturated fatty acids. Apparently there is merit in our making more use in our kitchens of unsaturated fatty acids.
To improve the health of young Canadians there is evidently a need to improve the health of all Canadians. Every young Canadian eventually becomes an adult. Because there is a constant example from one generation to the next, we must talk about the total population and the total society rather than single out an individual sector in a rather unrealistic and artificial manner. To do that we must co-ordinate the activities of the federal and provincial governments, industry, professional associations and community agencies. As we all know, a child does not live in isolation. Throughout life a child is influenced by his family, friends, peers, school, what is seen on television and by other messages which are impressed upon him in his daily life.
We cannot say there is one food pattern for all adult Canadians, just as we cannot say there is one desirable food pattern for all children. Therefore, a national nutrition program is built on the need to educate people about the kinds of choices they can make for nutritional health. That is what it really boils down to. When one goes into a grocery store, restaurant or different homes, one becomes very much aware of the number of food choices which can be made.
Bringing about a change in food habits to improve health is a long and slow task. However, it can be done, and in that sense the hon. member for Winnipeg North has done us a service in demonstrating that this House also can contribute to

bringing to the attention of the public the importance of this issue.
